title: Cap. VII: Christ–Adam comparison — meritorious proximity versus remote condemnation
pass_a_gloss: Garissoles's comparison-move: because Paul pairs Christ with Adam, Adam's disobedience should no more be called remote to condemnation than Christ's obedience is remote to justification. Placeus rejects the hidden premise that two first-in-kind causes of opposite effects may be compared only if both are equally proximate. Christ's obedience is known to be the full and sole ground of justification; Adam's disobedience is only a partial, incomplete ground of condemnation. Condemnation rests not solely on Adam's actual sin but also on inborn hereditary corruption and on our further actual and habitual sins; justification rests on Christ's single obedience and never on ours. Hence the justification ground, being unique, is at once first and near; the condemnation ground, sharing the work with many other causes, can be first without having to be near. Sin and condemnation arrive from Adam by natural propagation. The ancient Fathers and the early Reformers met Pelagian imitation with propagation of sin and did not need to mention imputation. Within that propagation Adam is first in the series, yet for each of us he is not the nearest or immediate cause. The sharp contrast: Adam is generation's most remote cause; Christ is regeneration's near cause. We are remote sons of Adam because many generations intervene; believers are near sons of Christ. Faith joins us to Christ directly, and so does his one Spirit shared by Christ and by us, with no intermediate person between Christ and the believer. Given that the learned man knew this, his wording is surprising. He ends by saying meritorious causes always involve proximity because the merit always works near (ἐγγύς) and with effect. Placeus calls that a showy proof: efficacy itself, like causality, admits remote versus near. Force belongs to each cause, and when the effect follows that force is efficacy; else it would not be a cause at all. Adam did propagate nature and corruption into us with real effect, yet remains only a remote cause of both. He is not himself the meritorious cause of our condemnation but the cause of that cause: hereditary corruption streamed from him as the near/immediate ground of condemnation, and Adam's actual sin caused that corruption. We cannot say the same of Christ — that his obedience caused some further virtue which then justifies us. Memorable difference: Christ's obedience is near to justification; Adam's disobedience is remote to condemnation because corruption stands in between. How then could Adam's actual sin be both meritorious and near as our condemnation's cause? If that sin is ours only by imputation, it earns our condemnation only through imputation's intervening act. So it is meritorious not through itself but only accidentally, by that divine, supernatural, voluntary imputing act; Christ's obedience, by contrast, is meritorious through itself, done on purpose by our surety in our stead. It would follow that our sinfulness and condemnation attach through themselves to that divine act and only accidentally to Adam's sin — a conclusion Placeus's conscience will not accept. Further: imputing sin to a man assumes he exists; condemning him to death assumes he lives. Our existing and living naturally precede condemnation, and of those Adam is only remote; so how is he proximate for the condemnation itself?
pass_b_english: "But," he says, "since a comparison is here instituted between Christ and Adam, the disobedience committed by Adam is no more to be called a remote cause of our condemnation than the obedience performed by Christ is to be called a remote cause of our justification." As if a comparison could not be instituted between two causes of opposite effects, when they are first in their kind, unless each alike is proximate! Who does not know that Christ's obedience is the adequate and only cause of our justification, but Adam's disobedience only an inadequate and partial cause of our condemnation? for we are condemned not on account of Adam's actual sin alone, but also on account of the hereditary corruption inhering in us, and all our other sins whether actual or habitual; whereas yet we are justified on account of Christ's one obedience, and in no way on account of ours. This cause, therefore, since it is the sole and only cause of justification, is the same both first and proximate; but that, since it is not alone, but together with it there are many other causes of condemnation, is first in such a way that there is no necessity that it be proximate. What? do we not draw sin and, through sin, condemnation from Adam by natural propagation? Did not both the Fathers of old and our first Reformers use to oppose the propagation of sin to Pelagian imitation, with no mention made of imputation? And yet of natural propagation, in its own kind indeed, Adam is the first cause, but of each of us the nearest or immediate cause he certainly is not. Here therefore the greatest difference is seen between Adam and Christ. Adam is the most remote cause of our generation, whereas Christ is the proximate cause of our regeneration. We are sons of Adam not nearest but remote: for between us and Adam many others are interposed; but we are nearest sons of Christ, as many as believe in him. For by faith we are united to Christ straight and immediately, and also by his Spirit, who, since he is only one in number both in Christ and in all of us, couples us to Christ so immediately that between Christ and the believer there is no middle person. Since the learned man was not ignorant of these things, how could he speak so? "Finally in meritorious causes," he says, "of the kind we are dealing with, there is always proximity, because that merit always acts near (ἐγγύς) and efficaciously." A fine argument! as if efficacy, like cause, could not equally be distinguished into remote and proximate! for each cause has its own force, and when the effect follows, that is efficacy; otherwise it would not be a cause. Did not Adam efficaciously propagate his nature and corruption into us? And yet he is only a remote cause of our nature and corruption. But he himself is not the meritorious cause of our condemnation, but the cause of this cause; for from him flowed the hereditary corruption that is the proximate or immediate cause of our condemnation, and of this the cause was Adam's actual sin. Can we likewise say that Christ's obedience was the cause of some virtue or obedience that is the cause of our justification? To that extent, therefore, there is a memorable difference between Christ's obedience and Adam's disobedience, and the former is to be called the proximate cause of justification, the latter the remote cause of our condemnation (for corruption is interposed). Otherwise how could Adam's actual sin be a meritorious and proximate cause of our condemnation? First, if it is not ours except by imputation, it does not merit our condemnation except by the intervention of imputation. It is therefore not a meritorious cause of our condemnation through itself, but only through an accident, by reason of that imputation, which is a divine action, and so supernatural and voluntary: whereas yet Christ's obedience is a meritorious cause of our justification through itself; namely, performed to that end and counsel by our surety in our place. That granted, it follows that our being sinners and being condemned is to be ascribed through itself to that divine action, but to Adam's sin only through an accident — which my conscience will in no way let me be led to believe or do. Next, he who imputes sin to some man presupposes that that man exists; he who condemns to death presupposes that he whom he condemns lives. Since therefore of our existing and living, which by nature precedes our condemnation, Adam is only a remote cause, how can he be the proximate cause of our condemnation?
source_text: Sed, inquit, cum hic instituatur inter Christum et Adamum comparatio, non magis dicendum est inobedientiam ab Adamo commissam, esse causam remotam nostrae condemnationis, quam obedientiam a Christo praestitam, esse causam remotam nostrae justificationis. Quasi vero non possit comparatio inter duas causas effectuum oppositorum institui, cum sunt in suo genere primae, nisi utraque sit pariter proxima! Quis nescit obedientiam Christi esse justificationis nostrae causam adaequatam et unicam, inobedientiam vero Adami condemnationis nostrae nonnisi inadaequatam et partialem? damnamur enim non ob solum peccatum actuale Adami, sed etiam ob inhaerentem nobis corruptionem haereditariam, et alia omnia nostra peccata sive actualia sive habitualia; cum tamen ob unam Christi obedientiam, nullo autem modo ob nostram, justificemur. Haec igitur, cum sola et unica justificationis causa sit, eadem et prima et proxima est; illa vero cum non sola sit, sed una cum ea aliae multae sint causae condemnationis, ita prima est, ut nihil necesse sit proximam esse. Quid? nonne peccatum et per peccatum condemnationem trahimus ab Adamo propagatione naturali? Nonne et Patres olim, et primi nostri Reformatores imitationi Pelagianae opponere solebant propagationem peccati, nulla imputationis facta mentione? Atqui propagationis naturalis, in suo quidem genere, prima est causa Adamus, sed cujusque nostrum proxima aut immediata profecto non est. Hic ergo maximum cernitur Adamum inter et Christum discrimen. Adamus est generationis nostrae causa remotissima, cum regenerationis nostrae Christus sit causa proxima. Filii sumus Adami non proximi sed remoti: inter nos enim et Adamum alii multi interjecti sunt; Filii vero Christi proximi sumus, quotquot in eum credimus. Per fidem enim unimur Christo recta et immediate, necnon per ejus Spiritum, qui cum unus tantum numero sit et in Christo et in omnibus nobis, nos Christo tam immediate copulat, ut inter Christum et fidelem intermedius nemo sit. Haec cum non ignoraret Vir Doctus, qui potuit sic loqui? Denique in causis meritoriis, inquit, quales sunt de quibus agimus, semper est proximitas, quia meritum illud semper ἐγγύς et efficaciter agit. Egregium argumentum! quasi non possit pariter efficacia, ac causa, distingui in remotam et proximam! sua enim cuique causae vis et, cum sequitur effectum, efficacia est; alioqui non esset causa. Annon Adamus efficaciter naturam suam et corruptionem in nos propagavit? Attamen naturae et corruptionis nostrae causa non est nisi remota. Non est autem ipse causa meritoria condemnationis nostrae, sed hujus causa causae; manavit enim ab eo corruptio haereditaria nostrae condemnationis causa proxima seu immediata, hujus autem causa fuit peccatum actuale Adami. Possumusne similiter dicere, obedientiam Christi causam fuisse alicujus virtutis vel obedientiae, quae sit causa justificationis nostrae? Eatenus igitur inter Christi obedientiam et Adami inobedientiam discrimen est memorabile, et illa proxima justificationis, haec remota condemnationis nostrae (corruptio enim interponitur) causa dicenda est. Alioqui quomodo peccatum actuale Adami causa esse posset condemnationis nostrae meritoria et proxima? Primum si non est nostrum nisi per imputationem, non meretur condemnationem nostram nisi imputationis interventu. Non est igitur causa meritoria nostrae condemnationis per se, sed per accidens tantum, ratione illius imputationis, quae est actio divina, atque adeo supernaturalis et voluntaria: cum tamen obedientia Christi sit causa meritoria justificationis nostrae per se; quippe, eo fine ac consilio a vade nostro loco nostro praestita. Quo posito sequitur, quod sumus peccatores et condemnamur, id esse divinae illi actioni per se ascribendum, peccato vero Adami nonnisi per accidens, id quod ut credam vel faciam adduci me mea nullo modo patitur conscientia. Deinde qui imputat alicui homini peccatum, supponit illum hominem esse, qui damnat ad mortem supponit eum quem damnat vivere. Cum ergo nostri esse et vivere, quod natura condemnationem nostram antecedit, non sit Adamus causa nisi remota, qui potest esse condemnationis nostrae causa proxima?
